population.note: FICTIONAL ESTIMATES. About 56.4M of ~265M US adults are on an incretin drug at end-2028 (21.3%); 27% have ever used one. Age-weighted check: 0.20×12 + 0.33×21 + 0.24×32 + 0.23×18 ≈ 21.2%. The jump at 65+ (9→18) comes from Medicare coverage becoming permanent; the jump at 50–64 comes from $0-copay generics in Medicaid and $45–69 cash generics. The income gap in who is on a drug is small (25/22/17, average 21.3). What separates the income groups is which drug they take and what goes with it. The top third is mostly on branded tirzepatide or retatrutide with strength coaching. The bottom third is mostly on generic semaglutide or oral starter doses. Roughly 29% of bottom-third adults with obesity have never used a drug, concentrated among the uninsured, people disenrolled from Medicaid under the 2027 work requirements, and rural counties without an FQHC pharmacy. Persistence improved because price stopped being the usual reason to quit. Cycling arithmetic: ever 27.0 − current 21.3 = 5.7 pts used-and-off-now; about 35% of current users have stopped and restarted at least once (0.35×21.3 = 7.5 pts), plus about 1.0 pt of those off now who had cycled before, so (7.5+1.0)/27.0 ≈ 31% of ever-users have cycled. That fits the parent's 36–47% within-year restart rate applied to the minority of stoppers who restart. Children: about 1% of under-18s (~0.7M), about 5% of children with obesity, still skewed to insured upper-income families, though Medicaid generic coverage for 12+ is narrowing the gap.

access.public_coverage: Public programmes are now the largest third-party payer, covering ~38% of the ~56.4M users. Medicare: ~11.0M users (the Bridge pilot was made permanent by statute in Jan 2028); generic semaglutide at $0 copay, branded drugs at the $245 negotiated price with a $50 copay. Medicaid: ~8.5M users in 44 states; generic $0 copay, branded drugs behind prior authorisation. VA/TRICARE/HRSA health-centre free provision: ~1.9M. Medicare arithmetic: 11.0M × (0.55 generic × $55 net + 0.45 branded × $245) = 11.0M × $140.5 × 12 ≈ $18.5B/yr. Medicaid: 8.5M × (0.80 × $45 + 0.20 × $245 = $85) × 12 ≈ $8.7B/yr gross (~$5.6B federal at ~65% FMAP). Total public incretin spend ≈ $27B/yr, well above the parent CBO path (≥$35B over 2026–2034). Generic price cuts offset only part of the volume growth.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India 60+ brands at ~$5–30/month and a major exporter; China launched domestic generics after its 2026 patent expiry; Canada generics ~CAD 60–90/month; Brazil, Mexico and Turkey generic markets established. Cost-plus generic injectable semaglutide is available in ~170 countries.
access.note: US generic semaglutide (injectable) launched Jan 2028 under the Sept 2027 Novo Nordisk patent settlement, which allowed licensed entry plus a Novo authorised generic. Cash prices are $45–69/month at cost-plus and big-box pharmacies. Tirzepatide has no generic. Branded list prices persist: Wegovy $1,349, and retatrutide launched at $1,399 list, which is the cash high. Employer coverage for weight management moved from 60% to 58% on the BGH measure, but ~70% of covering employers are generic-only with step therapy before tirzepatide. Payer mix of users: public ~38% (21.4M), commercial ~24% (13.5M), cash ~38% (21.5M). The cash figure includes ~3–4M adults buying imported Indian or Chinese pens and vials through personal-importation websites and social sellers, outside the DSCSA-serialised supply. That is the main counterfeit exposure.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic; US generic semaglutide from Jan 2028)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro; branded only)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, approved May 2028)
GLP-1 + amylin combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema, approved Jan 2027; modest uptake after REDEFINE-4)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide, mostly generic)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: alcohol use disorder: guideline-endorsed, not FDA-approved (ASAM Nov 2027: semaglutide as an option in AUD, strongest with comorbid obesity; Novo sNDA filed Feb 2028, decision 2029)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'metabolic health' / longevity low-dose generic semaglutide in people with BMI <27, via telehealth at $45–89/month; an estimated 4–5M adults, concentrated in affluent metros
craving and 'calm' protocols for alcohol, nicotine, gambling and compulsive shopping, sold as wellness programmes
alcohol reduction in people without obesity, following the AUD guideline
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
drugs.pipeline_note: Retatrutide BLA filed Feb 2027 and approved May 2028 (28.3% mean loss; dysesthesia in the label). CagriSema approved Jan 2027 but commercially marginal. The monthly_or_implant driver is honoured only within the approval rules. Amgen filed the MariTide (monthly injectable) BLA in Oct 2028 with a National Priority Voucher, and a decision is expected in 2029. No monthly or implantable incretin is on the US market at end-2028, and the 'monthly' that users talk about is anticipated, not available. Amycretin phase 3 topline is due 2029, so no filing yet. Survodutide was filed in Dec 2027, with a decision no earlier than Dec 2028 and none so far. Global incretin market ~$105B (2028). Novo's US revenue is shrinking from generic erosion; Lilly is growing on tirzepatide and retatrutide.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common class effect and the leading cause of discontinuation. Higher with retatrutide at escalation.
Elevated with rapid weight loss; rising absolute cholecystectomy counts track adoption.
No causal confirmation in long-term RCTs; absolute risk low.

~25–40% of weight lost is lean mass, depending on resistance training and protein intake. Clinicians now describe a 'generic-thin' sarcopenic pattern in older Medicaid and Medicare users without exercise support. Musculoskeletal and bone signals persist.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: CMS added optional DEXA/strength-assessment codes in 2028; no label change. Muscle-preserving adjuncts are still in trials.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FDA Sentinel and pooled Nordic and US claims analyses (2027) found a ~1.6–2× relative risk. The absolute risk is still small, roughly 1–3 extra cases per 10,000 person-years, but at ~56M users that is thousands of cases a year.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA class warning added to all GLP-1 receptor agonist and incretin labels (Jun 2027), with patient counselling on sudden painless vision loss. Ophthalmology screening is not mandated.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new evidence of a causal association.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the quiet')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The first survey estimates (2027–28 observational cohorts) put self-reported reduced pleasure or motivation at roughly 8–15% of users, dose-dependent. No RCT designed to measure it has read out. The same mechanism underlies the AUD benefit.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None on labels. FDA and FTC warning letters to telehealth brands marketing 'calm' and 'focus' claims.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The difference between trial and real-world figures persists. Cheap generics have turned regain into cycling rather than permanent stopping.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; supports the permanent Medicare coverage framing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Signals strengthening in older and low-income users and in normal-BMI wellness users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None; some state Medicaid programmes bundle a multivitamin.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; adolescents on decades-long therapy; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About six years of rigorous follow-up now exists. Cycling affects ~31% of ever-users and has no controlled data.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing requirements on retatrutide and CagriSema; NIH cycling cohort funded 2028.

safety_ledger.effect: Counterfeit, imported and compounded product harms (dosing errors, contamination, insulin-filled pens)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: CDC tallied ~2,400 ED visits and 11 deaths linked to non-serialised product in 2027–28. These include a spring-2028 cluster of counterfeit 'semaglutide' pens containing insulin, which caused severe hypoglycaemia, and endotoxin-contaminated vials. FAERS reports tied to non-FDA product passed 6,000.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA import alert on unregistered Indian and Chinese finished-dose semaglutide (Apr 2028); CBP seizures; DSCSA serial-number pen verification promoted to consumers. Personal importation still largely unenforced at the individual level.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Seen in retatrutide trials. Early post-launch reports are consistent with the trials.

food_and_beverage.state: With more than a fifth of adults and roughly a third of households on a drug, US snack and confectionery volume is down ~6–8% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~5%. The large packaged-food companies are cutting SKUs and selling divisions. Protein, fibre and single-serve formats grow. Store brands of 'GLP-1 companion' shakes are the fastest-growing grocery item among SNAP and Medicaid households. Revenue losses are tracking toward the low end of JPMorgan's $30–55B-by-2030 range.

alcohol.state: US spirits and beer volume is down ~7–9% from 2025, concentrated among the heavy drinkers who are most of sales. The AUD guideline turned drug-assisted cutting down into standard clinical advice. Diageo and Brown-Forman are cutting distillery shifts and pivoting to premium low-volume and non-alcoholic lines. Bars report fewer second rounds rather than fewer visits.

restaurants.state: Traffic is roughly flat and checks are smaller. Casual dining is shrinking its portions; fine dining sells tasting menus as events. Fast food is hurt most in suburban dinner dayparts. Small-plate and 'half portion' menus are now standard at chains.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists keep contracting, with store closures at Torrid and DXL. Mainstream brands profit from re-sizing. Premium athleisure cut to show a muscled, lean body is the fastest-growing segment and sells as an affluent uniform. Discounters sell loose-fit basics for the 'generic-thin'.

fitness.state: Strength training is the growth market: boutique strength studios, DEXA-scan memberships and on-drug coaching bundled with branded prescriptions. Budget gyms grow more slowly. The visible-muscle look is expensive in time and coaching, and that cost is what makes it read as status.

insurance.state: Generic semaglutide at $45–69 let employers keep coverage on a generic-only, step-therapy basis. Branded tirzepatide and retatrutide sit behind prior authorisation, and pharmacy trend has moderated to ~7%. Public programmes carry the volume: ~$27B/yr, which is now a federal budget line item.

pharma.state: The duopoly has split. Lilly leads branded volume with tirzepatide and retatrutide. Novo's US semaglutide revenue is falling under its own authorised generic and licensed generics. Generic makers (Teva, Viatris, Dr. Reddy's, Sandoz) earn low margins on very high volume. The global market is ~$105B and still growing on volume as prices fall.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being thin no longer tells you much, because generics made it cheap. The detail people read is muscle and skin: shoulders and forearms built by a trainer read as money, and a soft, slightly hollowed 'generic-thin' reads as public coverage. An unmedicated large body increasingly reads as rural, uninsured or deliberately refusing the drug.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The class line is set by income: who can afford coaching, protein, time to train and the premium drug, and who is covered at all after the Medicaid work requirements. In Scottsdale and on the Upper East Side, normal-weight professionals microdose for 'metabolic health' and train three times a week. In Dayton and the Rio Grande Valley, $0-copay generics are common among Medicaid enrollees who work on their feet and have no time to lift.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals continue at smaller sizes. Thanksgiving is a set of tasting plates. Office catering has shrunk to protein boxes. Among affluent users, eating a large meal off-drug has become a deliberate weekend indulgence, and some restaurants in Brooklyn and Austin run 'off-week' menus.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Dating apps (Hinge, Bumble) added optional profile tags for 'on/off/never' and medication choice, and users screen on them the way they screen on drinking. Couples where one partner is on-drug and quiet and the other is not are a recognised problem in couples therapy.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is now treated as something to manage. Wanting a lot of anything, food, drink or sex, is often taken as a sign of being unmedicated, and a minority defends it as authentic.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: Observational cohorts put self-reported reduced pleasure or motivation at ~8–15% of users, rising with dose. A larger share describe the same experience positively as 'quiet' or 'calm'. There is no RCT measurement, and manufacturers still say they have no data.
interior_life.framing: A feature with a brand name, 'the quiet'. Telehealth wellness brands sell low-dose generic semaglutide programmes as freedom from craving, calm and focus. The drug is prescribed off-label, and the marketing is framed around the programme rather than the drug, which keeps it just outside FDA and FTC reach. Clinicians still call it a side effect, and the AUD guideline calls it treatment. All three framings are in use at once.
interior_life.effect_on_work: Finance, sales and law firms do not mandate or pay for it, but productivity coaches and executive-health clinics recommend 'craving-free' protocols. Managers in some trading desks and consultancies report quieter, steadier teams with less after-work drinking. Some users report losing drive and dropping their dose before reviews.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Comedy about 'the quiet' is a stand-up genre. Some musicians who use say they write less. Loud, intense and sour flavours, extreme-spice menus and high-BPM club nights thrive as ways to get through the blunting. 'Off-week' parties in Brooklyn and Los Angeles are marketed as feral and unmedicated.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Reduced desire is the most-discussed complaint on forums. Couples therapists report mismatches between on-drug and off-drug partners. Some users take scheduled 'off weekends' to restore libido, which feeds cycling.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Mostly a talking point. A populist strand frames 'the quiet' as elites sedating workers and describes generic subsidies as pacification. A political consultant's claim that on-drug voters turn out less was widely shared and has not been replicated. The live political fight is over the ~$27B/yr in public spending and over disenrolled Medicaid adults losing $0 generics.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-access on price and coverage, and enforcement-heavy on supply. FDA added the NAION class warning (Jun 2027), approved retatrutide on schedule, and issued import alerts and DSCSA verification campaigns against counterfeits. It issues warning letters on 'calm/focus' marketing but has not banned off-label wellness prescribing.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: Subsidy, no mandate. Medicare obesity coverage was made permanent (Jan 2028) with a $0 copay for generic semaglutide and $50 for brands at $245. Medicaid offers $0-copay generics in 44 states with an enhanced federal match. HRSA funds free generic provision at community health centres for uninsured adults under 200% FPL (~0.9M users). TrumpRx lists generic semaglutide at $49.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Coverage still depends on BMI and comorbidity criteria. Branded drugs require prior authorisation and, in some Medicare Advantage plans, documented step therapy on the generic. Medicaid eligibility now depends on the 2027 work requirements, so losing a job can mean losing the $0 drug. Pharmacy pen serialisation creates a dispensing trail. There is no adherence monitoring.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army runs a pilot accepting recruits on generic semaglutide who meet body-composition standards, with a taper requirement before basic training. TRICARE covers generics. No civilian employer mandates.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: India and China dominate API and generic finished-dose production. US generic semaglutide relies on Indian API under the settlement. FDA import alerts target unregistered exporters, not licensed partners. The proposed Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs exempt generic incretins after lobbying by CMS and governors. The US–India price gap has narrowed from ~30× to ~3×.

events.event: FDA adds a class warning for NAION (sudden optic-nerve vision loss) to all GLP-1 and incretin labels after Sentinel and Nordic registry analyses find roughly doubled relative risk
Novo Nordisk settles semaglutide patent litigation with generic filers, licensing US entry from January 2028 and launching its own authorised generic. Cash prices open at $45–69 a month

ASAM guideline endorses semaglutide as a treatment option for alcohol use disorder. Within weeks, telehealth brands launch 'Quiet' craving-and-calm subscriptions for people without obesity, drawing FDA and FTC warning letters

With the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge pilot expiring, Congress makes Medicare obesity coverage permanent in an appropriations package. CMS sets $0 copays for generic semaglutide in Medicare and Medicaid, and HRSA funds free provision for uninsured low-income adults

CDC health alert after a cluster of severe hypoglycaemia cases traced to counterfeit 'semaglutide' pens filled with insulin and sold through social-media importers. FDA issues an import alert on unregistered Indian and Chinese finished-dose product
FDA approves Lilly's retatrutide (28% mean weight loss) at $1,399 list. In October, Amgen files its monthly MariTide injection using a priority voucher, with a decision due in 2029

open_tensions: The public now pays ~$27B a year for incretins, and coverage depends on Medicaid work requirements. Whether the subsidy is health policy or a cost to be cut is the 2028–29 budget fight.
The drug is cheap, but muscle, coaching and branded drugs are not. Bodies now show income more precisely than they did when the drug itself was scarce.

'The quiet' is sold as calm, prescribed for alcohol use disorder and reported as anhedonia. With ~56M users and no RCT measuring it, no regulator has decided whether it is a side effect, a benefit or a marketing claim.

Millions still buy non-serialised imported product to save $20–40 a month, and the monthly injection everyone is waiting for is not yet approved. Weekly cycling, counterfeits and the unknown long-term effects of on/off use all continue.
still_true: Tirzepatide (Zepbound/Mounjaro) has no US generic; Lilly's exclusivity is intact.
Medicare pays ~$245/month for branded GLP-1s under the 2025 Lilly/Novo deal, with a ~$50 beneficiary copay for brands.
Foundayo (orforglipron) remains on the market, with oral starter doses at $149 through TrumpRx.
The suicidal-ideation warning removed from Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels in Jan 2026 has not been reinstated.
Wegovy's list price is still $1,349, though almost no one pays it.

prose.headline: Thin Is Cheap Now. Muscle Isn't: How a $49 Generic Turned America's Bodies Into Pay Stubs
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2028, about one American adult in five takes an incretin drug, and for most of them it costs almost nothing. Generic semaglutide arrived in January under a patent settlement Novo Nordisk signed rather than keep losing ground to Lilly, Indian generics and Washington. It sells for $45 to $69 a month at cost-plus pharmacies. Medicare made its obesity pilot permanent the same month and set a zero copay for the generic. Forty-four state Medicaid programmes followed, and community health centres hand it out free to uninsured adults under twice the poverty line. Public programmes now cover nearly two in five users. The roughly $27 billion a year this costs has become a line in the budget fight.

Cheap drugs did not make bodies equal. The income gap in who takes the drug is narrow, about one in four adults in the top third and one in six in the bottom. What separates the groups is what comes with it. Affluent users take Lilly's tirzepatide or the new retatrutide, see a strength coach, get DEXA scans and buy fitted athleisure that shows the result. Medicaid users in Dayton or McAllen take the generic, stand all day at work and lose muscle along with fat. Clinicians call the pattern 'generic-thin'. Its counterpart, broad shoulders and a lean torso, has become the look of the professional class. A large body without medication now usually means someone the system missed: uninsured, rural, or dropped from Medicaid when the work requirements began.

The price collapse brought a second problem. Millions save twenty or thirty dollars by buying imported pens through social-media sellers, outside the serialised pharmacy supply. In spring, counterfeit pens filled with insulin sent people to emergency rooms with blood sugar near zero, and the CDC has now linked eleven deaths to unapproved product. The FDA answered with import alerts and a campaign urging people to scan their pens. Personal importation is still mostly unpoliced, because policing it means policing patients.

The drugs' risks have also become clearer. In mid-2027 the FDA put a class warning for sudden optic-nerve vision loss on every incretin label. The relative risk roughly doubles; the absolute risk is small, but with this many users it adds up to thousands of cases a year. Retatrutide carries a label for strange skin sensations. Nobody can yet say what six years of cycling on and off does, and almost a third of people who have ever used the drug have done it.

The flattening of appetite and pleasure that people once complained about as 'Ozempic personality' is now sold. Addiction physicians endorsed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder in late 2027. Within weeks, telehealth brands began selling low-dose generic programmes to normal-weight professionals as 'the quiet': calm, focus, freedom from craving. The FDA sends warning letters about the claims, but the prescriptions themselves are legal off-label. Consultancies do not require the programmes, though their coaches recommend them. Bars sell fewer second rounds, and spirits makers are closing distillery shifts. Comedians do whole sets about not wanting anything. Brooklyn nightclubs advertise 'off-week' parties for people who have skipped a dose to feel things again. Dating apps let users tag themselves on, off or never, and couples therapists now treat partners who are out of step on the drug.

The food industry is shrinking rather than collapsing. Snack volume is down by high single digits, portions are smaller, and protein shakes are the fastest-growing grocery item among SNAP households. Restaurants hold their traffic with half portions. Lilly is growing, Novo is shrinking, and generic makers make a small margin on enormous volume.

At the end of the year, Amgen filed for a once-a-month injection, with a decision due in 2029. Many people already talk as though the weekly dose is about to end. It is not on the market yet.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renee Holloway, fifty-three, sets her alarm for 5:10 and injects in the thigh before the coffee is done. Generic, from the Kroger on Wilmington Pike. Ohio Medicaid, zero dollars. Her daughter made her download the app, so she scans the pen box anyway. A green check.

Her first client is Mr. Albrecht in Oakwood. He is eighty-one and on the new one, the triple, with a trainer who comes Tuesdays. He is thinner than her and somehow bigger in the arms. She makes his eggs and eats half a banana standing at the counter. He asks if she's eating enough. She says she's never hungry, which is true.

At lunch her sister texts a link: forty dollars, Indian pens, ships in a week. Renee writes back, remember Darnell's cousin. Her sister sends an eye-roll.

In the afternoon she lifts Mrs. Pruitt from the bed to the chair and feels it in her lower back, the way she didn't used to. The pharmacist had handed her a sheet about protein. She buys the store-brand shakes, two for five, and drinks one in the car.

At home, Marcus is watching the game with a beer he has nursed since halftime. He started in March. They talk less in the evenings now, and it doesn't bother either of them.

At nine she reads the leaflet her new glasses came in: sudden painless vision loss, call right away. She covers one eye, then the other. The kitchen clock is still there. She goes to bed not having wanted anything all day.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The Army runs a pilot accepting recruits on generic semaglutide who meet body-composition standards, with a taper requirement before basic training.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: the parent says 'None' for workforce or military, and no driver or event leads to a military accession-policy reversal. It is asserted with no causal chain.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Children: about 1% of under-18s (~0.7M), about 5% of children with obesity
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude and mechanism: the parent had ~0.6% of children with obesity prescribed, so this is roughly an 8x rise in two years. The only mechanism offered is Medicaid generic coverage for ages 12+, which is a thin chain for that jump.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The jump at 65+ (9→18) comes from Medicare coverage becoming permanent
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism and magnitude: the pilot ran from Jul 2026 and permanence only arrived in Jan 2028, so most of the doubling predates it. The ~11.0M Medicare users also equals essentially all ~11M implied 65+ users, which leaves no room for commercial, cash or VA users in that age band.

rationale.badness: Cheap generics widen access and persistence, but the world carries real costs: 'generic-thin' sarcopenia in Medicaid and Medicare users, 11 counterfeit deaths, NAION cases in the thousands, and 8–15% self-reported reward blunting that no RCT has measured. Inequality moves from who gets the drug to bodies read as income, plus Medicaid work-requirement disenrolment (body_and_culture, population note). Cohesion and epistemic harms are the larger stories: couples out of step, 'the quiet' sold as a feature while clinicians call it a side effect, and no regulator deciding what it is. It is a harder society with new losers, not a refusal-level one.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: every driver is traceable to a field and an event. These include the Sept 2027 settlement, the Jun 2027 NAION label, the ASAM guideline and 'Quiet' brands, the Jan 2028 coverage and HRSA subsidy, the counterfeit insulin pens, and the MariTide filing, which respects the approval rules. mechanism: most chains are shown, but the Army pilot, the 5% pediatric jump and the attribution of the 65+ doubling to permanence are asserted (claims 1–3). 'Persistence improved because price stopped being the usual reason to quit' is also asserted, and event 2028-05 oddly contains an October filing. magnitude: adults on drug (21.3), ever used (27), income thirds (mean 21.3), age bands (~21.2), payer mix (21.4M public), and the Medicare ($18.5B) and Medicaid ($8.7B) arithmetic all reconcile and sit inside the envelope. Approval timing is allowed. Minor gaps remain: Medicare users equal all 65+ users, and the cycling note calls restarters 'the minority of stoppers' when 7.5 of ~13.2 stoppers is ~57%.
